name: Vending machine business
blurb: Buy machines, place them in busy spots, restock and split takings with the host
title: Vending Machine Business: How It Works, Costs and Risks
description: How a vending machine business makes money, what you need to start, who it suits, the scams to avoid and how to test a location before you buy a machine.
h1: How to start a vending machine business
answer: A vending machine business buys or leases machines, places them where people wait or work (offices, gyms, laundromats, factories) and earns the gap between what the snacks or drinks cost and what they sell for. It is often pitched as passive income, but most of the work is finding good locations, restocking and fixing jams, and a poor spot can leave a machine barely covering its own stock.

sections.h: How a vending machine makes money
body: Each sale earns the difference between the wholesale cost of the item and its price in the machine. Out of that you pay the location host (often a share of sales, sometimes a flat fee or nothing at all), card-reader fees, stock that expires, fuel for restocking runs and repairs.

Income depends almost entirely on foot traffic and how captive the audience is: a break room with no shop nearby sells far more than a lobby next to a convenience store. That is why operators talk about locations, not machines.

ul: A machine: new, used or refurbished. Used machines cost less but need parts and a working card reader, since many buyers no longer carry cash.
A location agreement in writing with the property owner or manager, saying who pays for power, the commission and how either side can end it.
Stock from a wholesale club or distributor, and a vehicle to restock.
Local paperwork: rules differ by country and city. In many places you need a business licence, and food or drink machines may need a permit or sales-tax registration; check with your local authority.
Insurance for the machine and public liability, plus a simple way to track sales per machine.

sections.h: Who it suits (and who it doesn't)

head: Suits
Not for
rows: People who like a route, a spreadsheet and small fixes
Anyone expecting money with no work
Someone with a few hours a week and a car
People without savings for a machine and a slow first months
Good networkers who can win a location
Areas with strict permits or no captive spots

ul: "Turnkey" packages: sellers who bundle overpriced machines with promised locations are a long-running scam pattern. Visit the location yourself and talk to the owner before paying.
Bad spots: a machine in the wrong place can sell so little that stock expires before it sells.
Theft and vandalism, mainly in public or unattended places.
A host can ask you to remove the machine at short notice; a written agreement with notice terms protects you.
Growth means more machines and more routes, so it scales with your time unless you hire help.

sections.h: How to test it cheaply first

ol: List ten places near you where people wait or work with no shop close by.
Ask three of the managers whether they would host a machine and on what terms, before you own one.
Count foot traffic at your best location at a few different times of day.
Price a used machine and a card reader, and cost a month of stock, fuel and commission.
Work out how many sales a day you need just to break even; if that number looks unrealistic for the spot, stop here.
Register the business and check the permits and taxes for food or drink sales where you live.
Sign the location agreement first, then buy one machine that fits that spot.
Stock a small mix, note what sells each week and drop what does not.
Keep a log of sales, stock costs and time spent per visit.
Only add a second machine once the first one covers its costs.

faq.q: Is a vending machine business really passive income?
faq.a: Not really. Machines need restocking, cleaning, cash or card settlement and the occasional repair, and the best locations have to be found and kept. It can be part-time, but it is a small route business, not money that arrives on its own.

faq.q: Should I buy a new or used vending machine?
faq.a: Used machines lower the cost of a first test, but check that parts are still available and that you can add a card reader. New machines cost more and make sense once you have a proven location.

faq.q: Where are the best places for a vending machine?
faq.a: Places where people wait or work for long stretches with nothing else nearby to buy from: break rooms, factories, gyms, laundromats, hospitals and some apartment buildings. Always ask the host first and get the terms in writing.
